edits.description: Make 'no agent can drive, run commands on or view any Mac' an explicit Gateway setting instead of a side effect of the Mac app not being installed, and write down the three ways to switch computer control off.
edits.how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config, and while no Mac node is wanted also every desktop host command the docs list as arriving with a Mac pairing: `system.run`, `system.run.prepare`, `system.which`, `browser.proxy`, `browser.proxy.upload.v1`, `mcp.tools.call.v1`, `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream`. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, matches exact command names, withholds the command (for `computer.act`, together with the node's `computer` capability) and is logged. The list is Gateway-wide, so the iPhone data commands from the phone-pairing entry (OCL-01) can go into the same wave-A change. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. Keep SSH-verified pairing off and do not use setup links for a Mac, since either can approve a node's first command surface automatically. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy; device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface; the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals gate shell commands on a node, not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload, with no restart); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility.

That denying browser.proxy and mcp.tools.call.v1 for nodes leaves the sandboxed research browser and any MCP servers on the Gateway itself untouched. No node is paired today; check right after the change.
caveats: Without this, once OpenClaw.app is installed on any family Mac, its pairing is approved and the macOS permissions are granted, pointer and keyboard control is available to any agent later given `computer` and to any caller with operator write access, because `computer.act` is in the macOS default allowlist and the app switch defaults on.
The deny list is global, not per Mac. The per-Mac controls are the pairing approval and the switch inside the app, so a pilot that lifts a deny entry lifts it for every paired node.
`screen.record` is already off unless explicitly allowed; `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream` are not, once a pairing that declares them is approved.
The two-step approval (device, then command surface) is not unconditional: SSH-verified pairing and setup-code enrollment can approve a node's first surface automatically.
The same pairing that would arm `computer.act` also brings shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream, which is why the deny list names those commands too.

edits.description: Give screen control a separate desktop to work on: a macOS virtual machine on the Mac mini with no Apple Account, no Messages and no saved passwords, reset before each run. Both model vendors tell developers to isolate computer use this way. As specified it is not yet clean: the guest still holds a signed-in gateway console and needs a route to the gateway, and the trifecta rule counts as met only after those gaps are closed.
caveats: The guest must still reach the gateway to act as a node. The gateway is bound to loopback and published only through Tailscale Serve, so the documented routes are an SSH tunnel into the host (which puts a host login inside the guest), joining the guest to the tailnet, or binding the gateway beyond loopback. Each changes the M0 baseline and needs its own review, so 'gateway only' is more than one firewall rule.

Node connections are not authenticated by Tailscale identity headers; the guest needs token-based node auth. A single-use pairing link avoids copying the shared gateway token but is documented for CLI node hosts; how the app pairs from inside a guest is untested.

The guest is not empty of secrets. OpenClaw.app inside it is signed in to the family gateway, and with shared-token auth that session is the shared owner profile; the agent that drives the guest's screen can open that Dashboard. Until the app is shown to run as a node with no operator rights, the clean desk contains access to everything it was built to keep away.

Anything tied to the family's Apple Account is unavailable by design: the Photos library, Notes and iPhone Mirroring. That removes many of the tasks people imagine, and every app Happy should operate has to be installed inside the guest.
A VM that is never reset is a shared, persistent desktop: leftovers from one run, or one parent, are there for the next. Plan a snapshot restore before each run.

Lume's unattended presets turn on SSH in the guest with published default credentials, and the tool has a telemetry setting. Change the password, turn SSH off and check telemetry before the guest touches the network.
Fallback with weaker isolation: a third standard macOS user on the mini with nothing signed in. It shares the machine and has to be the session on screen.

The roadmap already weighed a macOS VM for hosting the whole gateway and set it aside because a macOS guest cannot run the Docker sandbox. That does not block this narrower use, but it means no sandboxed tools inside the guest.
